Reddit (RDDT) stock trades at 26.5 times its adjusted earnings over the twelve months to June 30, 2026. This profit figure adds stock-based compensation, after tax, back to normalized net income. That is a high price for a single year of profit, and on analyst forecasts the multiple falls to 22.3 times by fiscal 2027. So what growth are buyers of Reddit stock counting on?

Reddit Investors Are Betting On Fast Sales Growth

Anyone buying at today's price is betting that Reddit will maintain rapid sales growth through fiscal 2027. The consensus forecast puts sales at $3.39 billion in fiscal 2026. For fiscal 2027, projections show sales rising another 32.5% while net income grows 22.8%, narrowing the forecast net margin to 29.9% from 32.3%.

On those forecasts, Reddit stock at $155.65 trades at 27.4 times fiscal 2026 earnings. Against the forecast for fiscal 2027, it trades at 22.3 times. Because the trailing 26.5 times figure adds stock-based compensation back into profit and the forecasts may not, the two metrics do not compare cleanly.

Reddit Has Been Growing Faster Than The Forecast

Reddit grew sales 66.6% over the twelve months to June 30, 2026, easily outpacing the consensus forecast for fiscal 2027. Advertising accounts for most of the business. Ad revenue hit $762 million in fiscal Q2 2026, up 64% from a year earlier. During the fiscal Q2 2026 call, management said that growth came from both pricing and impressions, and that active advertisers grew over 70%.

That growth is slowing, however. Sales grew 61.1% in fiscal Q2 2026, and management expects 47% to 49% growth in fiscal Q3 2026.

Where Could Reddit's Forecast Go Wrong?

The consensus forecast for fiscal 2027 is uncertain: the gap between the highest and lowest estimates of earnings per share equals 61.1% of the average forecast. The margin is one soft spot. Projections anticipate a 32.3% net margin in fiscal 2026. Reddit reported a 31.3% net margin over the twelve months to June 30, 2026, close to the forecast, though the forecast may not be on the same basis. If the margin slips back, the profit forecast for both years would come down.

Sales could also fall short if search traffic weakens. Management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call that search referrals were choppy in the quarter, and that Reddit's visibility on search remains low and is likely to stay volatile. Fewer visitors from search could mean fewer ad impressions, one of the two sources of growth management named, and the sales forecast would then come down.

title: Retirees Say This Drawdown Mistake Can Turn a Bad Market Into a Bigger Problem
detail:
Retirees Say This Drawdown Mistake Can Turn a Bad Market Into a Bigger Problem
Jennifer Taylor
Wed, October 21, 2026 at 10:00 AM MST 4 min read
RDDT
Trade Reddit on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
andreswd · iStock.com

Panic-selling is a classic move, and it's one of the most expensive. Retirees are especially exposed because they can't wait out a slump the way a 35-year-old can.

The average baby boomer has a 401(k) balance of $260,300 and an IRA balance of $286,700, according to Fidelity. While a grand total of $547,000 in retirement savings might sound like a lot, it can go fast if managed improperly.

Read Next: Worried about market swings? See why investors are moving to gold and silver IRAs

Find Out: FREE 2026 Investor Guide + Up to $25,000 in Silver with Qualifying Purchases

According to a Reddit thread, at least some retirees are looking ahead and creating a plan to avoid selling stocks in a downturn, by building cash or fixed-income safeguards. While this plan might not be perfect, it provides a much-needed peace of mind that helps them sleep at night.

The Sell-Low Trap

Worrying that the market will tank right after you stop working is common enough to have a name. Skee Orr, a certified financial planner (CFP) and founder of Kinetic Wealth, calls it sequence of return risk.

He said that two retirees can earn the same average return over a 20-year period, but end up in very different financial situations, depending on when a bad market hits.

"If a steep market decline hits early in retirement, while you are drawing money out to pay for living expenses, you may be forced to sell more shares at lower prices just to cover the basics," said Orr. "That action locks in losses and leaves fewer shares to recover when the market eventually bounces back."

In this case, the math works against you in ways it doesn't in other years, he said.

Build a Cash Cushion

To combat this, Orr said many proactive investors build a financial cushion — i.e., cash or more stable, lower-volatility assets — to draw from instead of stock investments, in the event the market goes through a rough stretch.

"This approach is more about peace of mind and staying power than theoretical perfection," he said. "If you can cover two or three years of living expenses using lower-risk resources without selling stocks, a down market becomes something you can wait out, rather than something that forces your hand."

Pitch a Bond Tent Before You Retire

Using a bond tent — gradually shifting a portion of a portfolio into bonds or other fixed-income assets — three to seven years before retirement is one practical approach Orr said some investors take.

"Think of it like filling a water tank before a dry season," he said. "It's not out of panic, but preparation."

title: Forget User Growth: Here’s the Real Reason Reddit’s Revenue Is Exploding
detail:
Forget User Growth: Here’s the Real Reason Reddit’s Revenue Is Exploding
Maham Fatima
Wed, October 21, 2026 at 8:15 AM MST 4 min read
RDDT
Trade Reddit on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Reddit (NYSE:RDDT) reports third-quarter results later this month, and the company has already told investors to expect revenue of $860 million to $870 million. That guidance follows a second quarter in which revenue grew 61%, the eighth straight quarter above 60%. But US daily active users rose only 6% to 53.2 million in the second quarter, while US revenue grew 56%. So American advertisers are paying far more for an audience that is barely getting bigger.

The company runs communities built around nearly every topic, where people ask questions, argue and trade advice, and it sells ads that appear next to those conversations. Its pricing power looks real and will probably keep paying off, though it rests on a US audience that is no longer growing quickly. Investors who want more high-growth stocks can find Reddit in our recent list 10 Best Future Stocks to Buy for the Next 5 Years.

Forget User Growth: Here’s the Real Reason Reddit’s Revenue Is Exploding
Advertisers Are Paying More Per User

The clearest proof is average revenue per user in the US, which reached $11.85 in the second quarter, up 51% from a year earlier. That jump explains why revenue outran the audience. Reddit's shareholder letter says advertising growth came from both higher pricing and more impressions, so advertisers are paying more for each ad as well as buying more of them.

Revenue has grown about 57% a year over the past five years, so the second quarter extended a long run instead of starting a new one. Costs have not run away either, since the operating margin sits at 28.25% over the past 12 months. For investors looking to add more fast growers, our list of 10 Best Aggressive Growth Stocks to Buy According to Wall Street Analysts is worth a look.

The US Audience Is the Weak Spot

Within that audience, the group that matters most is barely moving. US logged-in daily users, the people who sign in and tend to stay, rose just 1% to 23.1 million. Logged-out US users, who visit without an account, grew faster.

CEO Steve Huffman told shareholders in the second-quarter letter that search referrals were uneven during the quarter and more volatile toward its end. He added that product work helped offset that pressure, and that retention among new app users improved from a small base. That matters because search is one way new visitors find Reddit, so if it sends less traffic, fewer of them may ever become regulars. For someone holding the stock, that means owning a business whose profit growth depends on advertisers continuing to pay more for roughly the same American crowd. The worry caps the view instead of overturning it, since revenue and margins show no strain yet.

When deciding whether to buy, sell, or hold a stock, investors often rely on analyst recommendations. Media reports about rating changes by these brokerage-firm-employed (or sell-side) analysts often influence a stock's price, but are they really important?

Let's take a look at what these Wall Street heavyweights have to say about Reddit Inc. (RDDT) before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage.

Reddit Inc. currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.84, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 32 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.84 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy.

Of the 32 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 19 are Strong Buy and one is Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 59.4% and 3.1% of all recommendations.

Brokerage Recommendation Trends for RDDT
Broker Rating Breakdown Chart for RDDT

While the ABR calls for buying Reddit Inc., it may not be wise to make an investment decision solely based on this information. Several studies have shown limited to no success of brokerage recommendations in guiding investors to pick stocks with the best price increase potential.

Do you wonder why? As a result of the vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover, their analysts tend to rate it with a strong positive bias. According to our research, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations for every "Strong Sell" recommendation.

This means that the interests of these institutions are not always aligned with those of retail investors, giving little insight into the direction of a stock's future price movement. It would therefore be best to use this information to validate your own analysis or a tool that has proven to be highly effective at predicting stock price movements.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, which classifies stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), is a reliable indicator of a stock's near-term price performance. So, validating the Zacks Rank with ABR could go a long way in making a profitable investment decision.

Zacks Rank Should Not Be Confused With ABR

Although both Zacks Rank and ABR are displayed in a range of 1--5, they are different measures altogether.

The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.

Financial planners have long referenced the 4% rule, which caps first-year withdrawals at 4% of the portfolio balance. That guideline continues to evolve. Morningstar's 2025 "State of Retirement Income" report, published December 3, 2025, recommends a 3.9% starting withdrawal rate for retirees seeking steady, inflation-adjusted spending over a 30-year horizon. That figure rose from the 3.7% rate Morningstar published for 2024, driven by updated capital-market assumptions that blend top-down forecasts with bottom-up analyst inputs. One important qualification: the 3.9% base case applies to portfolios with an equity weighting of 20% to 50%. Heavier stock allocations actually produce a lower safe rate in Morningstar's model, because higher volatility offsets the expected return benefit. For retirees willing to accept some variability in annual spending, flexible withdrawal strategies combining a guardrails approach with delayed Social Security and Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities can support a starting rate as high as 5.7%.

Selling the home risks losing ACA subsidies if income exceeds $84,600, potentially raising health insurance premiums by 114% before Medicare eligibility at 65.

Options beyond selling include a reverse mortgage, an ADU on a child's property, or converting equity into annuities for guaranteed income.

A Reddit poster recently turned to the internet for advice about his parents. He is worried about their retirement outlook: they have almost no savings and are struggling to cover their basic bills.

He wants to know where they could realistically live and what concrete steps they should take to build some measure of financial security. Below is what the original poster (OP) shared, along with strategic options his parents can consider to build a more sustainable retirement despite their limited assets.

fizkes / Shutterstock.com
A workplace injury and a lack of retirement planning left the parents in crisis

According to the OP, his parents had limited formal education. His father suffered a disabling back injury at his farming job and was forced to stop working. He received a $100,000 settlement, a sum far too small to bridge the gap to Social Security eligibility, so the couple lived on it while waiting to qualify.

They now collect a combined $2,200 per month from Social Security. His mother earns a small amount babysitting, but opportunities are scarce in their rural town, and she spent years at home raising children rather than building a career. Because they never engaged in retirement savings, they have no nest egg and no pension from the father's former employer.

The parents carry a $1,500 monthly mortgage and a $300 car payment, and they simply cannot cover their bills on the $2,200 Social Security income plus the mother's occasional babysitting earnings. The OP is asking whether they should sell the home and, if so, where they should move to stretch their limited income as far as possible.

Strategic steps to create a sustainable retirement without savings
Andy Dean Photography / Shutterstock.com

Andy Dean Photography / Shutterstock.comAndy Dean Photography / Shutterstock.com

The OP believes his parents should sell the house, and that is likely the right starting point. He reports they have around $500,000 in home equity and are paying an expensive mortgage. Selling would free up that equity for investment. Morningstar's 2025 "State of Retirement Income" report, published December 3, 2025, found that 3.9% is the highest safe starting withdrawal rate for retirees seeking consistent, inflation-adjusted spending over a 30-year retirement, assuming a 90% probability of having funds remaining at the end. That figure is up from 3.7% in the prior year's report. At a 3.9% rate, $500,000 in proceeds could generate roughly $19,500 in additional annual income. Combined with Social Security, that would provide considerably more breathing room, particularly if the couple can secure housing for less than the $1,500 they currently pay. Morningstar's research also found that flexible withdrawal strategies can push the starting rate as high as 5.7% for couples willing to adjust spending in response to market conditions.
